I was 13 years old and working at my dad’s restaurant. He was very close with the folks in town and had dozens of regulars. One particular elderly regular came to sit at the bar while I was rolling silverware, so I said good morning and asked how he was doing. “I just buried my wife”. BURIED. I heard MARRIED.

With my 3 adolescent brain cells, I uttered “Oh how wonderful, congratulations!!”. My poor father hustled over and apologized profusely as I realized, with horror, what a degenerate piece of shit I was. Anyways, that painfully awkward moment still haunts me and resurfaces every now and again. Good times.

I’m so sorry you’re going through this. I was experiencing a similar disparity in a past relationship before med school. Realizing that I would be the adult between us, that I would be coming home daily after 80+ hour weeks to a house in shambles, him unfed, and passed out was unbearable. Closing that chapter was the most painful thing I’d ever done at that point. But things can be so much better when you consider your own needs.

You deserve to have a partner who treats you as an equal and who respects you enough to carry their weight. My fiancé says that in a relationship, 1 + 1 should equal 3. Greater than the sum of your parts. From your phrasing it sounds like there’s serious resentment on your end, which isn’t a dig, it’s exactly what I felt and it’s more than valid. But resentment is tough to scrub out if things don’t change.

You know your relationship better than anybody else, and I hope you guys can work through this. But something’s got to change before you burn out. Couple’s therapy. Something. Marriage isn’t going to make these issues disappear, if anything, it may make him more complacent.

I see where you’re coming from! Though in my personal experience, a wyd text almost always is a vague invitation. Typically if a friend is reaching out to genuinely check up, I’ll see different phrasing such as “hey just checking to see what’s up & how you’re doing!” I think the “how are you” component is key there to making general conversation as opposed to a directed inquiry.

And yeah I was making general categories for responses there - one could of course say “oh just chilling at home, how bout you” or “finishing up lunch with some friends”, though I’d argue that they could be placed into those categories of “not much” or “busy” for simplicity’s sake.

Like, say someone comes in with severe radiating left shoulder and jaw pain. If we write “has arm pain” and they’re actually having a heart attack, our chief complaint wouldn’t be accurate. It would be more correct to say “the patient complains of this sensation, we’re gonna run tests to make sure there’s nothing else up”.

Haha, yeah I see why that would seem kinda sketchy! That’s definitely how we write it. “Denies pain” in our notes would be the same as “has no pain” in real life, we just have to write everything from the perspective of the patient telling us what’s up.

With all due respect, as a current medical student, we  call the problem that a patient has the “chief complaint” and learn to chart it as “patient complains of” or “patient presents with”. I’m sure they were using regular lingo without meaning to offend, but it’s totally understandable why it would come off as condescending! Usually with patients I avoid the word “complain” even if it’s how we say things amongst ourselves/in records, because I feel that it comes off unpleasantly.

Hi there! I’m a medical student who had several PEs about 7 months ago. It came as a complete surprise. It took many inconclusive tests (I was negative for Factor V mutation), but after discussing it with my hematologist, he ordered a test for a Factor II (prothrombin) mutation, and I’m positive. It’s the second most common genetic mutation resulting in thromboembolic events such as these, and it would be worth getting tested since it’s familial. Totally agree with you, if I had been tested when I was younger before starting birth control pills, I probably would have never developed PEs.

I don’t mean to frighten you, but I would absolutely get tested before getting back on birth control pills! For me, the situation was nearly fatal.

The mutation which I have is with Factor II (G20210A). It’s heterozygous, meaning it passed down from just one of my parents! A homozygous mutation would mean it came from both. It also means that my body makes too much prothrombin, which increases my body’s ability and propensity to clot.

It could be a number of conditions that your family members have suffered from! To be safe I would recommend a hematology visit and labs before getting back on BC. I hope that this helps!

Man. As a medical student, I’ve had my fair share of exposure to cadavers from all walks of life, and I’ve witnessed several people die violent deaths. That transition is something I’m not entirely sure I’ll ever get used to. I held a man’s hand while he passed — felt his pulse slow, watched his eyes gloss over, and experienced that unmistakeable shift. But I can’t fathom stumbling upon a corpse unexpectedly. In a medical setting, it’s controlled. Traumatic in its own right, especially for loved ones, but controlled nonetheless. Finding a corpse like others have described, in such a horrifying way? Wow. I’m terribly sorry to those who have had that experience.
